questions.q: What makes a blockchain resistant to tampering with past transactions?
options: Each block contains a cryptographic hash of the previous block, so changing any past block would change its hash and break the chain of hashes for every block after it
Transactions are stored in a central government database
Blocks are encrypted with a password only the network administrator knows
Old blocks are automatically deleted after a fixed time period
questions.explain: Because each block's hash depends on the previous block's hash and contents, altering an old block changes its hash, which invalidates every hash pointer in every block that came after it — making tampering computationally obvious and expensive to hide.

questions.q: What is the core difference between Proof of Work and Proof of Stake consensus?
options: Proof of Stake requires more electricity than Proof of Work
Proof of Work requires miners to expend computational effort solving a puzzle to add a block; Proof of Stake selects validators based on the amount of cryptocurrency they've locked up as collateral
Proof of Work is used only by Ethereum; Proof of Stake is used only by Bitcoin
Proof of Stake has no way to penalize dishonest validators
questions.explain: PoW makes block creation costly in energy and hardware, so attacking the chain is expensive; PoS instead makes dishonesty costly by letting the network slash a validator's staked collateral, achieving security through economic risk rather than raw computation.

questions.q: What is the fundamental difference between symmetric and asymmetric encryption?
options: Symmetric encryption is always more secure than asymmetric encryption
Asymmetric encryption cannot be used for digital signatures
Symmetric encryption uses the same key to encrypt and decrypt; asymmetric encryption uses a mathematically linked key pair — a public key to encrypt (or verify) and a private key to decrypt (or sign)
Symmetric encryption requires a blockchain to function
questions.explain: Symmetric schemes need both parties to share one secret key, which is a distribution problem; asymmetric schemes solve that by using two mathematically related keys, so the public key can be shared openly while only the private key holder can decrypt or sign.

questions.q: When you sign a Bitcoin transaction with your private key, what does that signature prove to the network?
options: That the transaction has already been confirmed by miners
That the sender's account balance is sufficient, which the signature calculates directly
That the transaction is free of network fees
That the person broadcasting the transaction actually controls the private key corresponding to the public address the funds are being spent from, without ever revealing the private key itself
questions.explain: Digital signatures let you prove ownership of a private key by producing a signature only that key could generate, which anyone can verify against the matching public key — all without the private key ever being transmitted or exposed.

questions.q: What problem did Bitcoin's whitepaper solve that previous digital cash proposals couldn't?
options: The double-spending problem — preventing the same digital coin from being spent twice — without relying on a trusted central authority, using a distributed, timestamped chain of proof-of-work blocks
It solved the problem of encrypting emails between two parties
It was the first system to use public-key cryptography of any kind
It eliminated the need for any form of consensus among network participants
questions.explain: Earlier digital cash schemes either needed a trusted central server to prevent double-spending or couldn't prevent it at all; Bitcoin's breakthrough was combining a public, timestamped ledger with proof-of-work so a decentralized network of strangers could agree on which spend happened first.

questions.q: What is a smart contract on Ethereum?
options: A legal document that a lawyer uploads as a PDF to the blockchain
Code deployed to the blockchain that runs deterministically on the Ethereum Virtual Machine and automatically executes its logic when called, without a trusted intermediary
A type of cryptocurrency wallet used only for storing Ether
A centralized server that Ethereum validators use to store user data
questions.explain: A smart contract is just program code stored on-chain; because every node executes it identically on the EVM, its logic runs the same way for everyone, removing the need for a trusted third party to enforce the agreement.

questions.q: Why do Ethereum transactions require paying 'gas'?
options: Gas is a fixed subscription fee paid once per year per wallet
Gas fees are optional and only affect how the transaction looks in a block explorer

Gas is the fee that compensates the network for the computational work needed to execute a transaction or smart contract, and it protects the network from infinite loops or spam by capping how much computation a transaction can consume
Gas is paid to the sender of the transaction, not the network
questions.explain: Every opcode executed on the EVM has a gas cost; requiring gas both pays validators for the compute they provide and guarantees that a transaction, even a buggy or malicious one with an infinite loop, will run out of gas and halt rather than consume the network's resources forever.

questions.q: What does marking a Solidity function as `view` tell the compiler and the network?
options: The function can only be called by the contract owner
The function will automatically emit an event every time it runs
The function cannot accept any parameters
The function only reads blockchain state and does not modify it, so it can be called without submitting a transaction or paying gas (when called externally, off-chain)
questions.explain: Because a `view` function is guaranteed not to change any state, a node can simulate it locally and return the result immediately, letting external callers read contract data for free instead of broadcasting and paying for a full transaction.

questions.q: What is the purpose of a constructor in a Solidity contract?
options: It runs exactly once, at the moment the contract is deployed, typically to set initial state like the owner address or starting values
It runs every time any function on the contract is called
It is used to destroy the contract when no longer needed
It defines the contract's public ABI
questions.explain: The constructor executes only during deployment as part of the transaction that creates the contract, which makes it the natural place to initialize state that should be set once and never re-run, such as recording the deployer as the owner.

questions.q: In Solidity, what's the difference between `uint` and `int`?
options: `uint` is used for text strings; `int` is used for numbers
`uint` can only hold non-negative (unsigned) whole numbers; `int` can hold both positive and negative (signed) whole numbers
`int` can only be used inside a constructor
There is no difference — they are aliases for the same type
questions.explain: The 'u' in uint stands for unsigned, meaning the type's bits are entirely dedicated to representing magnitude with no sign bit, so it can only represent zero and positive values; int reserves a bit for sign, allowing negative values at the cost of a smaller positive range for the same bit width.

questions.q: Why does gas cost matter when writing a `for` loop in a Solidity smart contract?
options: Loops in Solidity execute off-chain for free and never cost gas
Gas cost only applies to `while` loops, not `for` loops

Every iteration executes EVM opcodes that consume gas, so a loop over an unbounded or attacker-controlled array can become prohibitively expensive or even exceed the block gas limit, causing the transaction to fail
The EVM automatically converts loops into a single flat-rate gas cost regardless of iterations
questions.explain: Because every opcode the EVM executes costs gas, a loop's total cost scales with the number of iterations; if that count is attacker-influenced (like the length of a public array), an attacker can grow it until the transaction can never fit under the block gas limit, effectively bricking the function.

questions.q: What actually happens when you compile a Solidity contract?
options: The compiler uploads your contract directly to a centralized Ethereum server
Compilation converts Solidity into JavaScript so it can run in a browser
Compilation is only a syntax check; no bytecode is produced
The compiler translates the human-readable Solidity source code into EVM bytecode (plus an ABI describing its interface), which is what actually gets deployed to and executed on the blockchain
questions.explain: Solidity is a high-level language that no blockchain node runs directly; the compiler's job is to produce low-level EVM bytecode that nodes actually execute, along with an ABI that tells external callers how to encode calls to the contract's functions.

questions.q: What is a Solidity `mapping`, and why is it a natural fit for representing token balances?
options: A mapping is a key-value store (like `mapping(address => uint256) balances`) that gives constant-time lookup from a key such as an address to a value such as a token balance, without needing to iterate a list
A mapping is an ordered array that must be iterated to find a value
Mappings can only store other mappings, never simple values
A mapping automatically syncs its data with an off-chain database
questions.explain: Token contracts need to look up 'how much does this address hold' constantly; a mapping gives direct, gas-efficient access by key instead of forcing a linear scan through an array of every holder, which would become unusably expensive as the holder count grows.

questions.q: What is the purpose of the `approve` and `transferFrom` functions in the ERC-20 standard?
options: They are used only to burn tokens permanently
`approve` lets a token holder authorize another address (like a smart contract) to spend up to a set amount on their behalf, and `transferFrom` is how that approved spender actually moves the tokens
They let anyone transfer any user's tokens without prior authorization
They are optional functions not included in the ERC-20 standard
questions.explain: This two-step pattern is what lets a decentralized exchange or other contract move your tokens on your behalf: you first call approve to grant a spending allowance, and the spender later calls transferFrom, which checks that allowance before moving any tokens.

questions.q: What does 'minting' a token mean?
options: Permanently destroying tokens and removing them from circulation
Transferring existing tokens between two wallets
Creating new units of a token and increasing the total supply, typically by calling a function restricted to an authorized address like the contract owner
Converting an ERC-20 token into an ERC-721 token
questions.explain: Minting increases total supply by creating brand-new tokens out of nothing on the ledger; because this can dilute existing holders' value, well-designed contracts restrict who is allowed to call the mint function, often with an onlyOwner-style modifier.

questions.q: What is the key structural difference between an ERC-20 token and an ERC-721 token?
options: ERC-721 tokens cannot be transferred between wallets
ERC-20 is used for NFTs, and ERC-721 is used for currencies
ERC-721 tokens do not require a smart contract to exist

ERC-20 tokens are fungible — every unit is interchangeable and tracked as a simple balance; ERC-721 tokens are non-fungible — each token has a unique ID and can represent a distinct, non-interchangeable asset
questions.explain: ERC-20 balances are just numbers, since one token is identical to another; ERC-721 instead tracks ownership per unique tokenId, which is what lets each token represent something distinct, like a specific piece of digital art or a specific deed.

questions.q: Why do many production tokens build on OpenZeppelin's ERC-20 or ERC-721 implementations rather than writing the standard from scratch?
options: OpenZeppelin's contracts are widely audited, tested, and battle-tested in production, reducing the risk of subtle bugs or security vulnerabilities that a hand-rolled implementation might introduce
OpenZeppelin contracts are required by the Ethereum protocol itself
Using OpenZeppelin removes the need to pay any gas fees
OpenZeppelin only supports tokens on the Bitcoin network
questions.explain: Reimplementing a token standard from scratch means re-discovering every edge case and vulnerability that's already been found and patched in a library that thousands of other contracts already rely on and that has been through extensive audits.

questions.q: Why does importing an OpenZeppelin contract like `ERC20.sol` into your own Solidity file help you build safer code faster?
options: Imports automatically deploy the imported contract to the same address on every network
You inherit pre-written, audited implementations of standard functionality (like transfer logic and access control) instead of re-implementing and re-testing that logic yourself
Importing a contract removes the need to compile your own contract
OpenZeppelin imports bypass the need for a Solidity compiler entirely
questions.explain: Inheriting from an imported contract gives your contract its functions and state handling for free, so you only need to write the logic that's actually specific to your token or application rather than re-deriving well-established standard behavior.

questions.q: What problem does a multi-signature (multisig) wallet solve that a normal single-key wallet doesn't?
options: It makes transactions completely free of gas fees
It allows the wallet's private key to be recovered if lost, with no other safeguards
It requires approval from multiple designated private keys (a quorum) before a transaction executes, so no single compromised or malicious key can move funds alone
It encrypts the blockchain itself so outside observers cannot see any transactions
questions.explain: By requiring, say, 3 of 5 authorized signers to approve before funds move, a multisig wallet removes the single point of failure a single private key represents — one stolen or lost key alone can't drain the wallet.

questions.q: What is a reentrancy attack, and how does the checks-effects-interactions pattern prevent it?
options: It's an attack where a validator refuses to include a transaction in a block, and the pattern fixes it by increasing gas limits
It's a bug in the Solidity compiler that checks-effects-interactions patches with a compiler flag
It's an attack unique to Proof of Stake networks that checks-effects-interactions has no effect on

A reentrancy attack occurs when an external call lets a malicious contract call back into the vulnerable function before its state is updated, often draining funds through repeated withdrawals; checks-effects-interactions prevents this by updating state (like reducing a balance) before making any external call
questions.explain: The DAO hack happened because a contract sent Ether to a caller before zeroing out that caller's balance, letting the caller's fallback function re-enter and withdraw repeatedly; doing the balance update first means any re-entrant call sees a balance that's already been reduced, so there's nothing left to steal.
